---
title: "Smart Pointers: `Box`, `Rc`, and `RefCell`"
description: "One Rust language concept taught with one short runnable example and a precise explanation."
---

## The question

**When is `String` ownership not enough?**

`Box<T>` puts a value on the heap with one owner. `Rc<T>` shares ownership **within one thread** using reference counting. `RefCell<T>` checks borrow rules **at runtime** for interior mutation.

## The rule to remember

Choose the smallest tool: `Box` for owned indirection, `Rc` for several owners in one thread, `RefCell` only when safe runtime-checked borrowing is necessary.

## The smallest complete example

Paste into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`. The [Rust examples page](examples/index.qmd) describes how to check all snippets automatically.

~~~rust
use std::rc::Rc;
fn main() {
    let a = Rc::new(String::from("hello"));
    let b = Rc::clone(&a);
    println!("{a} {b}"); // hello hello
}
~~~

**Follow the state:** `a` and `b` are two smart-pointer handles referring to one shared String allocation. `Rc::clone(&a)` increments the reference count; it does not clone the String itself. Both handles can read the same value.

## Important limitation

`Rc<T>` is **not** thread-safe. Use `Arc<T>` across threads. `RefCell<T>::borrow_mut()` can panic if an incompatible borrow is active; it does not disable the borrowing discipline.
